Occlusion then facilitated the need for a dynamic camera, [music] which in turn demands the ability to rotate, something that did not play nice with the Pixel Pipeline. [music] A goal moving forward was to stick [music] with the static camera and design the building blocks in a way where they were less likely to block. Now, taking this vanilla Unity scene using the straight out of the box Universal Pipeline, [music] we can start by first passing our scene to the low-resolution render texture needed for our camera system. From here, we can start to add back in the passes, quantization, cloud coverage, outlines, [music] and god rays. And when we add all of these features back in, the pipeline [music] is back up and running. As we build more and more of the game out, the hope is that we'll slowly hone down on a palette that works well for this style of game. With our world now a blank canvas, we have the opportunity to populate it with objects and props that aim to bring the world to life. A major goal with Tower Keep is to create a living world full of emerging properties. If we look at games like Noita, despite the standard pool of items being fairly contained, every run feels different due to how the world reacts. World materials have varying properties that, when combined in various ways, lead to interesting outcomes. And whilst the actual behaviors are simple, the world generation does the heavy lifting to place you in incredibly varied scenarios. >> [music] >> Now looking back at Tower Keep, whilst it will take time to achieve that level of cohesion, we can start looking at how we want to build our world. In a dynamic path tower defense, I guess one of the most important properties might be something like blocking. That is, whether enemies are capable of pathing through the object. If we take a look at our first starting biome, the grasslands, we could look at trying to add something like vegetation or flora to the world. Trees naturally make sense as a solid object to be something that can block the enemy's path. And grass feels like something which grows in these areas that would not stop enemies from traversing their path. Now, these objects can be extended with additional behaviors, such as whether they're targetable. It feels like grass is maybe something wispy that [music] cannot be directly hit. Whereas a tree is a structure that can be demolished, and when destroyed, opens up the path for enemies, leaving a stump behind. >> [music] >> During a previous episode, we looked at generating flow fields and giving the player the ability to shape the path. In this version of the game, we want to continue that, but recontextualize it to make sense with the flavor of this world. Now, instead of our blockers being made of plastic bricks, [music] we can look at building our walls from different materials, things like wood and stone, all resources that can be gathered from the environment. >> [music] >> A tree could be chopped, its material gathered, and then a wood wall can be constructed. >> [music] >> And this sort of wraps up what I want to capture in this game. Using the land and resources available to you, almost as if it's its own character. So, this is where we're currently headed. Tower Keep is a cross between tower defense and survival craft genres, with a focus on emergent world dynamics. >> [music] >> I'm really keen to know what you think and looking forward to hearing your thoughts and ideas in the comment section.
